source.title: Superposition Is Not Necessary: A Mechanistic Interpretability Analysis of Transformer Representations for Time Series Forecasting

page_placements.theme: SAE features have condition-dependent causal and steering utility

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study argues against a sparsity-penalty artifact as the explanation for its lack of superposition signatures, and reports a sparsity calibration sweep. It does not directly analyze SAE reconstruction-error structure.
record.gate_note: The paper tests SAE dictionary expansion, latent interventions, and sparsity calibration in PatchTST. Those measures do not test linear predictability of the reconstruction error, per-token error scaling or context overlap, comparisons with same-size random errors, a linear/nonlinear error split, or whether SAE-derived analyses lose behavior. The calibration sweep bears on only the sparsity-penalty part of V6; other proposed training or architecture artifacts are not tested.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs on PatchTST FFN activations to probe for superposition. It does not measure SAE error structure: no linear prediction of the error, no per-token error norms or context overlap, and no random-error baseline. It has no linear/nonlinear split and no analysis with versus without the error term. Its sparsity sweep reports only L0, not error or dark matter. Its 'not an artifact' claim concerns the absence of superposition, not SAE dark matter. It also does not cite the original source. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that superposition is not necessary for competitive forecasting on standard benchmarks. They take this to suggest the benchmarks have low representational demand, helping explain why linear models such as DLinear stay competitive. The 'not an artifact of the sparsity penalty' claim refers to the absence of superposition, not to SAE error.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE reconstruction replacement, dictionary scaling, latent amplification, and sparsity calibration on a time-series forecasting transformer; it does not analyze the error-vector predictability or per-token error behavior described in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported SAE sparsity calibration varies λ; the main dictionary-scale analysis compares 0.5×, 1.0×, and 4.0× dictionaries.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing activations with SAE reconstructions changes forecasting MSE by under about 3%. The 0.5× vs 4.0× difference averages 0.214% (Table 1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In small time-series transformers, SAE reconstruction replacement costs little downstream, and dictionary size barely changes that cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Amplifying the top-10 latents 5× shifts forecasts by about 0.031 MAE on average, 0.061 at most.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Dominant SAE latents in PatchTST FFN activations have weak individual causal influence on forecasts.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing the 4.0× SAE's sparsity penalty λ raises L0 smoothly; the 4.0× dictionary has higher L0 than the 0.5× one at every λ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latent activity responds to the sparsity penalty as expected in time-series FFN activations.

record.problems: The study probes only post-GELU FFN activations; attention and residual-stream representations are not analyzed. It uses a fixed random seed per configuration and reports no uncertainty estimates. It does not compare SAE reconstruction effects with random perturbations or directly analyze reconstruction-error structure.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 reports per-dataset and per-horizon degradation, dead-latent percentages, and causal shifts; Table 2 reports reconstruction MSE and L0 per dataset and horizon. These detailed values are not extracted as separate rows because they do not measure the claim versions' error properties. Table 3's per-dataset and per-λ L0 values are summarized in r3 using the paper's explicit across-dataset description.

untested.parts: All: no linear prediction of SAE error from activations.
Per-token error predictability and same-context failure across sizes. Table 2 gives only aggregate reconstruction MSE at 0.5×, 1.0× and 4.0×.
No comparison of SAE-reconstruction harm with random errors of the same norm.
No decomposition of the error into linear and nonlinear parts.
No circuit or steering analysis with versus without the error term.
No measure of error or dark matter across sparsity penalty, architecture, dead latents, shrinkage or end-to-end training. The λ sweep reports L0 only.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 limits_scope label is removed: L0 alone cannot bear on whether SAE error reflects training artifacts. Table 2 shows aggregate reconstruction MSE falling but nonzero from 0.5× to 4.0× (e.g., Traffic H=96: 0.0346 to 0.0272). This is too coarse, and covers too small a size range, to test V2's per-token and scale claims. No uncertainty is reported, and each configuration uses a single seed.

versions.untested_parts: No linear prediction of the SAE error from input activations is measured.
No per-token error-norm predictability, token/context overlap across SAE sizes, or error behavior with scale is measured.
The study measures forecasting changes under SAE reconstruction, but does not compare them with random errors of the same size.
No linear versus nonlinear decomposition of SAE error, or analysis of what either part represents, is performed.
No circuits, steering analyses, or other SAE-feature-based analyses are compared with and without the error term.

The sparsity-penalty calibration is tested through latent activity, but the paper does not measure whether dark matter/error structure changes across penalties. Shrinkage, dead-latent effects on error, alternative architectures, and end-to-end training are not tested.

rows.operation_detail: Sweep SAE sparsity penalty λ and report average active latents per token (L0).

conditions.value: Weather, Electricity, Traffic, Exchange, ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTm1, ETTm2

rows.measure: Average L0, active latents per token.
rows.value: As λ decreases, L0 increases smoothly across all datasets for both dictionary sizes; the 4.0× dictionary has higher L0 than the 0.5× dictionary at each λ.
rows.note: The paper interprets the calibration as evidence that its null result is not an artifact of the fixed sparsity penalty. The sweep reports latent activity, not whether SAE error structure or downstream effects change with λ.
rows.check: The λ sweep reports only L0 (Table 3). It does not measure reconstruction error, its structure, or downstream effects across λ, so it cannot show whether dark matter shrinks with training choices. The authors' artifact argument concerns superposition, not SAE error. Unlink from V6.

relation.reason: It discusses related SAE reconstruction and functional sensitivity questions without testing error predictability, matched random errors, error retention in analyses, or training explanations of dark matter.

tranche.reason: The study probes superposition through dictionary scaling, latent utilization, and amplification. It neither tests nor uses any of the six SAE dark-matter claims.

source_check.notes: Latent amplification does not compare analyses with versus without the SAE error term. The sparsity calibration concerns absent superposition signatures, not whether SAE dark matter is a training artifact.
